about.author: Zyphullen
about.certainty_rule: green = established (known science, or a defined / proved result in Maths); orange = leading idea / partial progress; red = unknown / open problem. A link takes the colour of its less-certain end.

suggest_a_fix.subject: Echo Atlas fix: <Card name> (<card id>)
suggest_a_fix.note: Every card has a Suggest a fix button that opens a prefilled e-mail (section, card, card id, version, page link). Card ids: fntu/<id>, maths/<id>, history/<id>-<n>, cell/<id>, body/<id>, planet/<id>, element/<symbol>, <section>/link/<from>><to>.

about.what_this_file_holds: Organs, bones, muscles, vessels and nerves, and which kinds of cell build each part.
about.how_to_use: Every item has id, title, certainty, summary, details and sources (title, url, type). Full source details (year, link check) are in sources_used. A link's reason_sources are the sources on its two cards. Fact-check against the sources; flag anything that looks wrong or out of date.

virtual_body.title: Human body
summary: About 1.65 m tall here, close to the average adult height worldwide.
Made of about 30 trillion human cells.
details: Proportions follow standard adult measurements: the head is about 1/7.5 of the height, the navel about 60% of the way up.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Front view; one typical body, real people vary a lot.

sources.title: Sender et al. 2016: Revised Estimates for the Number of Human and Bacteria Cells in the Body (PLoS Biol)
Ncd Risk Factor Collaboration (NCD-RisC) 2016: A century of trends in adult human height (eLife)
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 1.2 Structural Organization of the Human Body

virtual_body.title: Skin
summary: Your largest organ: about 1.6–1.8 m² and 3–4 kg.
It keeps water in and germs out.
details: Epidermis: about 0.1 mm thick (up to 1.5 mm on the soles).
Dermis: about 1–4 mm, with collagen made by fibroblast cells.
Under it is a fat layer (hypodermis) of varying thickness.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Shown as a smooth outline with no surface detail.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 5.1 Layers of the Skin

virtual_body.title: Face
summary: Eyes, nose, mouth and ears: most of the senses sit in the head, close to the brain.
details: The face has about 20 small muscles that make expressions.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Simple outline, not a portrait.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 11.3 Axial Muscles of the Head, Neck, and Back

virtual_body.title: Breast
summary: Made of fat, supporting tissue and the mammary gland, on top of the chest muscle (pectoralis major).
They develop at puberty; size and shape vary a lot between people and are not linked to how much milk they can make.
details: In pregnancy the breasts grow and prepare to make milk.
After birth they make milk to feed the baby.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Simple contour lines, typical adult size.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 27.2 Anatomy and Physiology of the Ovarian Reproductive System

virtual_body.title: Nipple and areola
summary: The nipple has several tiny openings (often about 5–10) where milk ducts end.
The darker ring around it is the areola, typically 3–6 cm across.
details: Small glands in the areola (Montgomery glands) keep the skin moist.
In pregnancy the areola often gets darker and larger; a newborn finds it more easily.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Drawn as plain circles.

virtual_body.title: Collarbone (clavicle)
summary: A long S-shaped bone you can see and feel under the skin, from the top of the breastbone to the shoulder.
It links the arm to the trunk.
details: It is the first bone to start hardening in a growing embryo, about 5–6 weeks after fertilisation.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Surface line only.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 8.1 The Pectoral Girdle

virtual_body.title: Knee (front)
summary: The kneecap (patella) sits in the tendon of the thigh muscle, in front of the knee joint.
It protects the joint and helps the thigh muscle straighten the leg.
details: The kneecap is still soft cartilage at birth and turns to bone at about 3–6 years old.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Simple outline of the kneecap.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 9.6 Anatomy of Selected Synovial Joints

virtual_body.title: Mons pubis
summary: A rounded pad of fat over the pubic bone, at the front of the vulva.
It cushions the pubic bone; hair grows here after puberty (not drawn).
details: The creases at each side are the groin (inguinal) folds, where the thigh meets the trunk.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Simple outline with light shading.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 27.2 Anatomy and Physiology of the Ovarian Reproductive System

virtual_body.title: Navel (umbilicus)
summary: A scar where the umbilical cord was attached before birth.
details: In the womb the cord carried blood between the baby and the placenta: food and oxygen in, waste out.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 1.6 Anatomical Terminology

virtual_body.title: Vulva (external genitals)
summary: The outer parts: the mons pubis, the outer and inner lips (labia majora and minora), the clitoris, and the separate openings of the urethra (for urine) and the vagina.
The labia protect the openings.
details: At birth the baby comes out through the vaginal opening, which stretches a great deal.
Shown here in a simple front view; much of it is hidden between the thighs when standing.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Simplified clinical outline; inner parts not drawn in detail.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 27.2 Anatomy and Physiology of the Ovarian Reproductive System

virtual_body.title: Mammary glands
summary: Each breast has about 15–20 lobes. Each lobe has many small lobules that can make milk.
Ducts carry milk from the lobes to the nipple.
details: In pregnancy hormones (oestrogen, progesterone) grow the ducts and lobules.
After birth the hormone prolactin starts milk production; oxytocin squeezes milk out when the baby feeds (the let-down reflex).
virtual_body.drawing_note: Lobes and ducts drawn as a simple pattern.

virtual_body.title: Vagina
summary: A stretchy muscular tube about 7–10 cm long, from the cervix to the outside.
Menstrual blood leaves the body through it.
details: It is the birth canal: in childbirth it stretches to let the baby through.
Helpful bacteria (lactobacilli) keep it acidic, about pH 3.8–4.5, which protects against infection.
virtual_body.drawing_note: It runs up and backwards, so from the front it looks much shorter; shown over the bladder so you can see it.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 27.2 Anatomy and Physiology of the Ovarian Reproductive System

virtual_body.title: Cervix
summary: The narrow lower end of the uterus, about 2.5–3 cm long, opening into the vagina.
It makes mucus that changes through the monthly cycle.
details: In pregnancy it stays closed with a mucus plug that protects the baby.
In labour it opens (dilates) to about 10 cm so the baby can be born.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 27.2 Anatomy and Physiology of the Ovarian Reproductive System

virtual_body.title: Fallopian tubes
summary: Two tubes about 10–12 cm long from the uterus towards the ovaries.
Their finger-like ends catch the egg when it is released.
details: Fertilisation (egg meets sperm) usually happens inside the tube.
Tiny hairs (cilia) move the early embryo to the uterus over about 3–5 days.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 27.2 Anatomy and Physiology of the Ovarian Reproductive System

virtual_body.title: Skull
summary: 22 bones; 8 make the braincase around the brain.
The jaw (mandible) is the only one that moves.
details: Adult skull is about 18–20 cm from front to back.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 7.2 The Skull

virtual_body.title: Spine (vertebral column)
summary: 33 vertebrae: 7 neck, 12 chest, 5 lower back, then the fused sacrum (5) and tailbone (about 4).
It holds the spinal cord.
details: In an adult woman it is about 60–70 cm long.
Seen from the front it is mostly hidden behind the organs.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 7.3 The Vertebral Column

virtual_body.title: Rib cage
summary: 12 pairs of ribs. The top 7 join the breastbone (sternum) directly.
Pairs 11 and 12 float free at the front.
details: It protects the heart and lungs and moves with every breath.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Rib curves simplified.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 7.4 The Thoracic Cage

virtual_body.title: Sternum (breastbone)
summary: A flat bone about 15–17 cm long in the middle of the chest.
details: Three parts: manubrium, body and the small xiphoid process.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 7.4 The Thoracic Cage

virtual_body.title: Clavicle (collarbone)
summary: Joins the breastbone to the shoulder blade.
About 14–15 cm long in women.
details: One of the most commonly broken bones.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 8.1 The Pectoral Girdle

virtual_body.title: Humerus
summary: The upper arm bone, about 30 cm long in women.
details: Its round head fits the shallow shoulder socket, so the shoulder moves a lot but dislocates easily.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 8.2 Bones of the Upper Limb

virtual_body.title: Radius and ulna
summary: The two forearm bones. The radius is on the thumb side.
The radius turns around the ulna to rotate your palm.
details: About 22–25 cm long.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 8.2 Bones of the Upper Limb

virtual_body.title: Hand bones
summary: 27 bones: 8 wrist bones (carpals), 5 metacarpals, 14 finger bones (phalanges).
details: Both hands together hold over a quarter of the body’s bones.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Wrist bones shown as one group.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 8.2 Bones of the Upper Limb

virtual_body.title: Pelvis
summary: Two hip bones plus the sacrum, forming a ring.
In women it is wider and rounder, making room for childbirth.
details: The female pelvic inlet is oval and wide; the angle under the pubic bones is usually over 80°.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Outline simplified.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 8.3 The Pelvic Girdle and Pelvis

virtual_body.title: Femur (thigh bone)
summary: The longest and strongest bone: about 42–45 cm in a 1.65 m adult (about 26–27% of height).
details: It slants inward to the knee; the slant is larger in women because the pelvis is wider.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 8.4 Bones of the Lower Limb

virtual_body.title: Patella (kneecap)
summary: A bone that grows inside the tendon of the thigh muscle.
details: About 5 cm across.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 8.4 Bones of the Lower Limb

virtual_body.title: Tibia and fibula
summary: The shin bone (tibia) carries the weight; the thin fibula is on the outside.
details: The tibia is about 35–37 cm long in women.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 8.4 Bones of the Lower Limb

virtual_body.title: Foot bones
summary: 26 bones: 7 tarsals, 5 metatarsals, 14 phalanges.
details: Seen from the front, the foot is foreshortened.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Foot shown foreshortened and simplified.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 8.4 Bones of the Lower Limb

virtual_body.title: Brain
summary: About 1.2–1.3 kg in adult women, with about 86 billion neurons.
Uses about 20% of the body’s energy.
details: How it makes thoughts and feelings is still being worked out.

sources.title: Azevedo et al. 2009: Equal numbers of neuronal and nonneuronal cells make the human brain an isometrically scaled‐up primate brain (J. Comp. Neurol.)
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 13.2 The Central Nervous System

virtual_body.title: Eye
summary: About 24 mm across.
The retina has about 120 million rods and 6 million cones.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 14.1 Sensory Perception

virtual_body.title: Thyroid gland
summary: A butterfly-shaped gland in the neck, about 5 cm wide.
Its hormones set how fast the body uses energy.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 17.4 The Thyroid Gland

virtual_body.title: Lungs
summary: The right lung has 3 lobes, the left has 2 and a notch for the heart.
About 300–500 million air sacs (alveoli).
details: At rest you breathe about 12–16 times a minute, about 0.5 L each time.
Their inner surface is about 50–75 m².

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 22.2 The Lungs

virtual_body.title: Heart
summary: About the size of a fist, 250–300 g in women.
Beats about 60–100 times a minute; shown at 70.
details: Pumps about 5 litres of blood a minute at rest.
It sits in the middle of the chest, tilted to the person’s left.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Outline simplified. Zoom in to see the 4 chambers and 4 valves (textbook cut-away).

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 19.1 Heart Anatomy

virtual_body.title: Right atrium
summary: Collects oxygen-poor blood from the body through the two venae cavae.
Holds the sinoatrial node, the heart’s natural pacemaker.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Textbook cut-away (coronal section), simplified. In real life the right ventricle faces the front and the left atrium sits at the back.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 19.1 Heart Anatomy

virtual_body.title: Right ventricle
summary: Pumps oxygen-poor blood to the lungs through the pulmonary valve.
Wall about 3–5 mm thick; pressure about 25 mmHg when it squeezes.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Textbook cut-away (coronal section), simplified. In real life the right ventricle faces the front and the left atrium sits at the back.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 19.1 Heart Anatomy

virtual_body.title: Left atrium
summary: Collects oxygen-rich blood from the lungs through 4 pulmonary veins.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Textbook cut-away (coronal section), simplified. In real life the right ventricle faces the front and the left atrium sits at the back.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 19.1 Heart Anatomy

virtual_body.title: Left ventricle
summary: Pumps oxygen-rich blood to the whole body through the aorta.
Thickest wall, about 1 cm; pressure about 120 mmHg when it squeezes.
details: About 70 mL leaves it each beat at rest.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Textbook cut-away (coronal section), simplified. In real life the right ventricle faces the front and the left atrium sits at the back.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 19.1 Heart Anatomy

virtual_body.title: Septum
summary: The wall between the left and right sides, so the two bloods do not mix.
details: Carries the electrical bundle that makes the ventricles squeeze together.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Textbook cut-away (coronal section), simplified. In real life the right ventricle faces the front and the left atrium sits at the back.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 19.1 Heart Anatomy

virtual_body.title: Tricuspid valve
summary: 3 flaps between the right atrium and right ventricle.
Shown opening while the ventricle fills, shutting when it squeezes.
details: Its closing (with the mitral valve) is the first heart sound, “lub”.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Textbook cut-away (coronal section), simplified. In real life the right ventricle faces the front and the left atrium sits at the back.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 19.1 Heart Anatomy

virtual_body.title: Mitral valve
summary: 2 flaps between the left atrium and left ventricle.
Shown opening while the ventricle fills, shutting when it squeezes.
details: Its closing (with the tricuspid) is the first heart sound, “lub”.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Textbook cut-away (coronal section), simplified. In real life the right ventricle faces the front and the left atrium sits at the back.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 19.1 Heart Anatomy

virtual_body.title: Pulmonary valve
summary: 3 half-moon flaps from the right ventricle to the lungs’ artery.
Shown opening when the ventricle squeezes.
details: Its closing (with the aortic valve) is the second heart sound, “dub”.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Textbook cut-away (coronal section), simplified. In real life the right ventricle faces the front and the left atrium sits at the back.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 19.1 Heart Anatomy

virtual_body.title: Aortic valve
summary: 3 half-moon flaps from the left ventricle into the aorta.
Shown opening when the ventricle squeezes.
details: Its closing (with the pulmonary valve) is the second heart sound, “dub”.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Textbook cut-away (coronal section), simplified. In real life the right ventricle faces the front and the left atrium sits at the back.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 19.1 Heart Anatomy

virtual_body.title: Liver
summary: The largest internal organ, about 1.2–1.5 kg.
Mostly on the person’s right, under the ribs.
details: Does over 500 jobs, from cleaning blood to making bile.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 23.6 Accessory Organs in Digestion: The Liver, Pancreas, and Gallbladder

virtual_body.title: Gallbladder
summary: A small bag under the liver that stores bile, about 50 mL.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 23.6 Accessory Organs in Digestion: The Liver, Pancreas, and Gallbladder

virtual_body.title: Stomach
summary: J-shaped, on the person’s left under the ribs.
Holds about 1–1.5 L after a meal.
details: Its acid has a pH of about 1.5–3.5.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 23.4 The Stomach

virtual_body.title: Spleen
summary: About 11 cm long, on the person’s left behind the stomach.
Filters old red blood cells and helps fight infection.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 21.1 Anatomy of the Lymphatic and Immune Systems

virtual_body.title: Pancreas
summary: About 15 cm long, behind the stomach.
Makes digestive juices and insulin.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 23.6 Accessory Organs in Digestion: The Liver, Pancreas, and Gallbladder
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 17.9 The Endocrine Pancreas

virtual_body.title: Kidneys
summary: Two bean shapes about 11 cm long at the back of the belly.
Together they filter about 180 L of blood plasma a day.
details: The right kidney usually sits a little lower, under the liver.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 25.3 Gross Anatomy of the Kidney

virtual_body.title: Small intestine
summary: About 3–5 m long in a living person.
Where most food is absorbed.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Coils drawn as a simplified pattern, not each real loop.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 23.5 The Small and Large Intestines

virtual_body.title: Large intestine
summary: About 1.5 m long, framing the small intestine.
Takes water back and holds trillions of gut bacteria.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 23.5 The Small and Large Intestines

virtual_body.title: Bladder
summary: Stores urine: usually 300–500 mL.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Drawn see-through so the reproductive organs behind it show.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 25.2 Gross Anatomy of Urine Transport

virtual_body.title: Uterus
summary: A pear-shaped muscular organ about 7–8 cm long, behind and above the bladder.
Each month its lining thickens; if there is no pregnancy, the lining is shed as a period.
details: In pregnancy the early embryo implants in the lining and the placenta forms.
The uterus grows from about 60 g to about 1 kg and holds the baby for about 40 weeks.
In labour its strong muscle contracts to push the baby out.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 27.2 Anatomy and Physiology of the Ovarian Reproductive System

virtual_body.title: Ovaries
summary: Two almond-sized glands, about 3–4 cm long, either side of the uterus.
They hold the eggs and make the hormones oestrogen and progesterone.
details: A baby girl is born with about 1–2 million immature eggs; only about 400–500 are released in a lifetime, usually one a month.
After an egg is released, the corpus luteum makes progesterone, which supports an early pregnancy.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 27.2 Anatomy and Physiology of the Ovarian Reproductive System

virtual_body.title: Skeletal muscles
summary: About 600 muscles, roughly 30–35% of body weight in women.
They pull on bones through tendons.
details: Only the larger surface muscles are drawn.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Main surface muscles only, shapes simplified.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 10.2 Skeletal Muscle
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 11.2 Naming Skeletal Muscles

virtual_body.title: Deltoid
summary: The rounded shoulder muscle; lifts the arm sideways.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 11.5 Muscles of the Pectoral Girdle and Upper Limbs

virtual_body.title: Pectoralis major
summary: The large fan-shaped chest muscle; pulls the arm forward and across.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 11.5 Muscles of the Pectoral Girdle and Upper Limbs

virtual_body.title: Biceps brachii
summary: Bends the elbow and turns the palm up.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 11.5 Muscles of the Pectoral Girdle and Upper Limbs

virtual_body.title: Forearm muscles
summary: About 20 muscles that move the wrist and fingers.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 11.5 Muscles of the Pectoral Girdle and Upper Limbs

virtual_body.title: Rectus abdominis
summary: The long belly muscle, split into sections by bands of tendon.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 11.4 Axial Muscles of the Abdominal Wall, and Thorax

virtual_body.title: External oblique
summary: The side belly muscle; twists and bends the trunk.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 11.4 Axial Muscles of the Abdominal Wall, and Thorax

virtual_body.title: Sternocleidomastoid
summary: The neck muscle that turns and tilts the head.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 11.3 Axial Muscles of the Head, Neck, and Back

virtual_body.title: Quadriceps
summary: Four muscles at the front of the thigh that straighten the knee.
details: One of the strongest muscle groups in the body.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 11.6 Appendicular Muscles of the Pelvic Girdle and Lower Limbs

virtual_body.title: Sartorius
summary: The longest muscle in the body, crossing the thigh diagonally.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 11.6 Appendicular Muscles of the Pelvic Girdle and Lower Limbs

virtual_body.title: Adductors
summary: Inner-thigh muscles that pull the legs together.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 11.6 Appendicular Muscles of the Pelvic Girdle and Lower Limbs

virtual_body.title: Tibialis anterior
summary: Lifts the front of the foot.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 11.6 Appendicular Muscles of the Pelvic Girdle and Lower Limbs

virtual_body.title: Gastrocnemius (calf)
summary: The calf muscle; lifts the heel through the Achilles tendon.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 11.6 Appendicular Muscles of the Pelvic Girdle and Lower Limbs

virtual_body.title: Arteries
summary: Carry blood away from the heart (red here).
The aorta is about 2.5–3 cm wide.
details: Blood in the aorta moves on average about 20 cm/s; the moving dots use that speed.
All arteries together are roughly 9,000–19,000 km long (newer estimates); the old "100,000 km" figure counts every vessel and is too high.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Main arteries are mapped; the small branches that appear as you zoom are a generated pattern, not a map.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 20.1 Structure and Function of Blood Vessels

virtual_body.title: Aorta
summary: The biggest artery, about 2.5–3 cm wide.
It arches over the heart and runs down in front of the spine.
details: It splits into the two iliac arteries at about the navel.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 20.5 Circulatory Pathways

virtual_body.title: Veins
summary: Carry blood back to the heart (blue here; real blood is always red, darker in veins).
details: Valves stop blood falling back down the legs.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Main veins drawn; small branches are a generated pattern.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 20.1 Structure and Function of Blood Vessels

virtual_body.title: Nerves
summary: Nerves carry signals between the brain, spinal cord and body.
Fast nerve signals travel up to about 120 m/s.
details: The moving dots are shown much slower than real so you can see them.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Main nerves drawn; small branches are a generated pattern. Signals slowed down.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 13.4 The Peripheral Nervous System

virtual_body.title: Spinal cord
summary: About 43 cm long in women; ends near the first lumbar vertebra.
Below that, nerve roots continue as the "horse’s tail" (cauda equina).

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 13.2 The Central Nervous System

virtual_body.title: Sciatic nerve
summary: The thickest nerve, up to about 2 cm wide, running down the back of the thigh.
details: Seen from the front it lies behind the femur.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 13.4 The Peripheral Nervous System

virtual_body.title: Arm nerves
summary: The median, ulnar and radial nerves run down the arm to the hand.
Hitting the ulnar nerve at the elbow is the "funny bone".

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 13.4 The Peripheral Nervous System
